title: Gyoza
subtitle: pan-fried pork and cabbage dumplings
excerpt: Gyoza are Japanese pan-fried dumplings filled with pork, cabbage and ginger. They are cooked using the steam-fry method: browned on the bottom, then steamed under a lid, then finished to crisp the base again. Makes about 30 dumplings, serving 4.
sourceNotes: Gyoza are the Japanese version of Chinese jiaozi dumplings, introduced to Japan after World War II. They became wildly popular and now differ from their Chinese cousins in being thinner-skinned, more garlicky and always pan-fried.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze uncooked gyoza on a tray until solid, then transfer to a bag. Cook from frozen, adding 2 extra minutes to the steaming stage.
recipe.batchNotes: Double or triple the filling and fold a large batch. Freeze in portions for quick weeknight meals.

glossaryTerms.definition: Japanese pan-fried dumplings with a thin wheat wrapper. They are cooked using the steam-fry method which gives them a crispy bottom and tender top.
A cooking technique where food is first fried to brown one side, then water is added and a lid goes on to steam the food through, and finally the lid is removed to re-crisp the base.

content.text: different from regular fried dumplings. The dumpling gets a crispy bottom, then is steamed to cook the filling through, then dried out again for a final crisping. The wrapper needs to be bought ready-made or made from flour and boiling water. Serves 4.
Squeeze as much water as possible from the cabbage before mixing the filling. Wet filling will make the wrappers soggy and the gyoza will burst during cooking.

items.prepNote: very finely shredded then squeezed dry

content.text: Make the wrappers: pour the boiling water into the flour and mix with chopsticks or a fork until it comes together. Knead for 5 minutes into a smooth dough. Cover and rest for 20 minutes. Roll into a thin sheet and cut into 9cm circles, or divide the dough into 30 pieces and roll each individually.
Combine all filling ingredients in a bowl. Mix vigorously with chopsticks or a spoon until the mixture becomes slightly sticky.
Place 1 teaspoon of filling in the centre of each wrapper. Dampen the edges with water. Fold and pleat to seal. Press the base flat so the gyoza can stand upright.

Heat 1 tbsp oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat. Arrange gyoza flat-side down in the pan. Fry for 2 minutes until the bottoms are golden. Add 60ml water to the pan and cover immediately with a lid. Steam for 4 minutes.

Remove the lid and let all the water evaporate. Drizzle another 1 tsp oil around the edge of the pan. Fry for 1 more minute until the bottoms are very crispy. Slide onto a plate and serve with dipping sauce.

attrs.cause: Filling was too wet or the wrapper seal was poor
attrs.fix: Squeeze the cabbage very hard in a clean cloth before mixing. Press the pleated edge firmly to seal.

attrs.cause: Not enough resting time or the dough was over-kneaded
attrs.fix: Rest the dough for at least 20 minutes. Hot water doughs need rest to soften and become pliable.

attrs.symptom: Gyoza stick to the pan and tear
attrs.cause: Not enough oil or the pan was not hot enough before the gyoza went in
attrs.fix: Heat the oil until shimmering before adding gyoza. Do not move them until it is time to steam.

content.text: Gyoza are eaten across Japan at home, in ramen shops and izakaya. Hamamatsu in Shizuoka is Japan's self-declared gyoza capital. The city eats more gyoza per person than anywhere else in Japan. The home-made version takes effort the first time but becomes faster with practice. Many Japanese families make a large batch together and freeze half for the week ahead.
